lead: At microwave frequencies a multimeter cannot read a voltage that changes every few millimetres along a line. The bench instead measures quantities that stand still: the standing-wave pattern on a slotted line (giving VSWR, guide wavelength and load impedance), the heating effect of power, the resonance of a cavity (giving frequency), and, with a vector network analyser, the complex S-parameters themselves. Every component in the earlier chapters is checked this way before it goes into a system.
prereq: You need: Γ, VSWR and the standing-wave pattern (see Reflection coefficient, standing waves and VSWR), guide wavelength in a rectangular guide, and S-parameters and directional couplers.

sections.h3: Slotted line: VSWR, wavelength and load impedance

blocks.text: A slotted line is a length of waveguide (or coaxial line) with a thin slot along the centre of its broad wall, where it cuts no wall current. A small probe dips through the slot, samples the electric field, and feeds a crystal detector and meter. Sliding the probe maps the standing wave set up by the load.
VSWR S = V<sub>max</sub>/V<sub>min</sub>,   |Γ| = (S − 1)/(S + 1),   λg = 2 × (distance between adjacent minima)
blocks.where: V<sub>max</sub> and V<sub>min</sub> are probe readings proportional to field strength; minima are λg/2 apart. Minima are sharper than maxima, so they are used for positions.

blocks.text: A crystal detector at low level is square-law: its output follows RF power, so a meter reading M goes as V². If the meter is calibrated in voltage (the VSWR meters on lab benches are), use the readings as they are. If it reads power, take square roots first: S = √(M<sub>max</sub>/M<sub>min</sub>) and |Γ| = (√M<sub>max</sub> − √M<sub>min</sub>)/(√M<sub>max</sub> + √M<sub>min</sub>).

Frequency follows from λg: for the TE₁₀ mode, 1/λ₀² = 1/λg² + 1/λc² with λc = 2a. Load impedance: replace the load by a short and mark a minimum (a point a whole number of λg/2 from the load plane); refit the load and measure how far the minimum moves towards the load, dmin. Then
z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>L</sub>/Z₀ = (1 − jS tan βd<sub>min</sub>) / (S − j tan βd<sub>min</sub>),   β = 2π/λg
blocks.where: d<sub>min</sub> is the distance from the load to the first voltage minimum. The same result comes from the Smith chart: go d<sub>min</sub> towards the load from the r = 1/S point on the real axis.

blocks.text: High VSWR (above about 10): the minimum is too shallow to read against the maximum, and a square-law detector cannot cover the range. The double-minimum method measures the width W between the two points either side of a minimum where the detector reads twice the minimum power; then S ≈ λg/(πW).

items: Bolometer or thermistor mount: a small resistor whose resistance changes with temperature forms one arm of a self-balancing bridge. With no RF, the bridge supplies DC current I₁ to hold the element at its balance resistance R. RF heating then lets the bridge reduce the current to I₂ to keep R. The RF power equals the DC power removed: PRF = (I₁² − I₂²)R. This DC substitution makes the method absolute.

Thermocouple sensor: RF power heats the hot junction of a thin-film thermocouple; the emf comes from the temperature difference between the hot and cold junctions and is proportional to the absorbed power.
Diode sensor: fast and sensitive (down to about −70 dBm), square-law at low level and linear at high level.
High power: measure a known fraction through a directional coupler and fixed pads, then add back their dB values; at very high power a water-load calorimeter measures the heat directly.

blocks.text: Attenuation and insertion loss are measured by substitution: read the power with a direct connection (P₁), insert the device, read again (P₂); A = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₂) dB. Reflection with a reflectometer: two couplers facing opposite ways sample the incident and reflected powers, and |Γ| = √(Prefl/Pinc).

Frequency: a cavity wavemeter is a high-Q cavity tuned by a micrometer plunger and coupled to the line. When it is tuned to the signal it absorbs power and the detector reading dips; the calibrated dial gives the frequency. An electronic counter with a prescaler or a down-converter reads frequency digitally to many digits; a spectrum analyser shows it with the spectrum.

sections.h3: Vector network analyser and SOLT calibration

blocks.text: A vector network analyser (VNA) sends a swept test signal into one port and uses directional couplers to separate the incident, reflected and transmitted waves. Receivers measure their amplitude and phase, and the instrument divides them: S₁₁ = b₁/a₁, S₂₁ = b₂/a₁, then the same with the source switched to port 2. It shows the matrix of S-parameters and the scattering matrix directly, in magnitude and phase, over frequency.

Raw readings carry systematic errors: finite coupler directivity, the source and load match of the test ports, and frequency tracking of the receivers (12 error terms for a full two-port). Calibration measures known standards at the reference plane and solves for those terms. SOLT uses a Short (Γ = −1), an Open (Γ = +1), a matched Load (Γ = 0) at each port, and a Thru connecting the ports; TRL (thru, reflect, line) suits on-wafer and waveguide work. After calibration the VNA corrects every sweep; check it with a known airline or pad before trusting a measurement.

examples.question: A WR-90 slotted line (a = 22.86 mm) is used with a voltage-calibrated VSWR meter. With an unknown load: V<sub>max</sub> = 3.0, V<sub>min</sub> = 1.2, adjacent minima are 19.9 mm apart, and the first minimum is 6.0 mm from the load. Find the VSWR, |Γ|, the return loss, λg, the frequency and the normalised load impedance.
steps: λg = 2 × 19.9 = 39.8 mm. (The old trap: λg is never 19.9 mm.)
λc = 2a = 45.72 mm. 1/λ₀² = 1/39.8² + 1/45.72² = 6.313 × 10⁻⁴ + 4.784 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.1097 × 10⁻³ mm⁻², so λ₀ = 30.02 mm and f = c/λ₀ = 9.99 GHz. Note λg > λ₀, as in any hollow guide.
examples.answer: S = 2.5, |Γ| = 0.429, RL = 7.36 dB, λg = 39.8 mm, f = 9.99 GHz, z<sub>L</sub> = 0.896 − j0.892 (a capacitive load).

examples.question: (a) A bolometer bridge with R = 200 Ω carries 10 mA with no RF and 8.5 mA after RF is applied. Find the RF power. (b) A transmitter line is sampled by a 20 dB coupler followed by a 30 dB pad, and a power meter reads 2.5 mW. Find the transmitter power.
steps: Add back the coupling and the pad: 3.98 + 20 + 30 = 53.98 dBm.
examples.answer: 5.55 mW from the bolometer; the transmitter delivers 53.98 dBm = 250 W.

traps: Taking the distance between adjacent minima as λg. It is λg/2.
Square-rooting readings from a voltage-calibrated VSWR meter, or not square-rooting power readings. Check how the meter is calibrated first.
Finding λg smaller than λ₀ in a waveguide. In a hollow guide λg > λ₀ always; a smaller value means a reading error.
Measuring a high VSWR from V<sub>max</sub>/V<sub>min</sub> directly. Above about 10 use the double-minimum method, S ≈ λg/(πW).
Trusting uncalibrated VNA data. Without SOLT (or TRL) correction, directivity and port match errors can make a good part look bad or a bad part look good.

quiz.q: Define VSWR and relate it to |Γ|.
quiz.a: VSWR = V<sub>max</sub>/V<sub>min</sub> on the standing wave; |Γ| = (S − 1)/(S + 1), and S = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|).
Bolometer or thermistor (DC substitution in a bridge), thermocouple, and diode detector; a water-load calorimeter for very high power.

quiz.q: Why must power readings from a square-law detector be square-rooted before computing VSWR?
quiz.a: The detector output follows power, which goes as V². VSWR is a ratio of voltages, so S = √(M<sub>max</sub>/M<sub>min</sub>).

quiz.q: What do the standards of SOLT calibration do?
quiz.a: Short (Γ = −1), Open (Γ = +1) and Load (Γ = 0) at each port fix the reflection error terms (directivity, source match, reflection tracking); the Thru fixes load match and transmission tracking. The VNA solves for the error terms and removes them from every later sweep.

quiz.q: A power-calibrated detector reads 9 mW at a maximum and 1 mW at a minimum. Find the VSWR and |Γ|.
In the double-minimum method, the twice-minimum points are 1.0 mm apart and λg = 39.8 mm. Find the VSWR.
quiz.a: S ≈ λg/(πW) = 39.8/(π × 1.0) = 12.7 (the exact formula √(1 + 1/sin²(πW/λg)) gives 12.7 too).

quiz.q: A student reads 20 mm between adjacent minima in a WR-90 line at 10 GHz and writes λg = 20 mm. What is wrong?
quiz.a: Adjacent minima are λg/2 apart, so λg = 40 mm. Also λg must exceed λ₀ = 30 mm in a hollow guide; 20 mm is impossible. The theoretical value is 39.76 mm.

quiz.q: Why is an uncalibrated VNA sweep not acceptable for a final S₁₁ measurement?
quiz.a: The raw data include directivity leakage, port mismatch and tracking errors comparable to a good part's S₁₁. With a raw directivity of 25 dB (an error wave of 0.056), a load with 30 dB return loss (|Γ| = 0.032) could read anywhere from 21.1 dB to 32.2 dB. Only a calibration at the reference plane makes the result meaningful.

beyond: Modern labs use electronic calibration modules, on-wafer probes for MMICs, and time-domain gating to look at one discontinuity at a time. Search for "TRL calibration" and "electronic calibration module".
